chapters.label: Intro
chapters.text: Happy Tuesday, it's November 24th. A Spurs win to start us off, then a FIFA boss who lives on a jet, a tech billionaire with a very awkward résumé update, and a satellite with a name straight out of 1957. Let's go.

chapters.label: 🏆 My Teams
chapters.text: The Spurs handled the Kings last night, 123 to 107, and they're now 15 and 3. Stephon Castle did a little of everything: 28 points, 8 rebounds and 11 assists. That's a near triple-double from a guy who looks like he's having fun. Fifteen and three. Just sit with that for a second.

chapters.label: 🏈 Sports
chapters.text: The SEC is now openly talking about throwing LSU out of the conference. The league announced in a legal filing that its presidents and chancellors will meet December 3rd, two days before the SEC Championship Game, to consider terminating LSU's membership. This all goes back to RJ Luis and LSU's push to roster former professional players, which has already produced lawsuits in state and federal court. Here's the wrinkle. The SEC passed a penalty system this summer, with a half-season coach suspension and fines up to half a sport's annual budget. But a Louisiana judge's injunction means the league admits it has no avenue to penalize LSU for playing Luis. So the conference that can't fine you is reportedly considering just evicting you. It takes a two-thirds vote, and expulsion is still considered unlikely, but sources say some presidents are angry enough to vote yes. That's a long way from a stern letter.

chapters.label: 🏈 Sports
chapters.text: Thirty-nine private jet flights in a hundred and fifteen days. That's FIFA president Gianni Infantino, according to a BBC Sport analysis, and it works out to one flight every three days. He visited 32 countries, racked up more than a hundred thousand air miles, and spent nearly nine full days in the air. The clock starts July 28th, when news broke that he planned to sell off a stake in the World Cup. He's up for re-election next March, and critics say the frequent flying looks a lot like campaigning, since FIFA has no rules on campaign funding. FIFA says it's just the president's duty to keep up relations with its 211 member associations. Funny how that duty doubled his country count from last year. He's now seen as the favorite, partly because his rivals couldn't find a candidate until the last minute. Meanwhile, the planet is sending its regards.

chapters.label: 💻 Tech
chapters.text: Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia, the company whose chips power basically the entire AI boom. That's eleven days after he resigned over allegations of two affairs, one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Pillow talk with a suspected spy, at the company making the chips the US and China are racing over. That's not a scandal, that's a supply chain risk. The board decided he's the right person to lead, and now Republicans and Democrats are both objecting to Trump's role in bringing him back. Congress is expected to question Huang about his China ties and about that intervention. Huang has spent years polishing a family-man, American Dream image, and his fortune has already slid from close to two hundred billion dollars to around a hundred and five billion. Nobody gets that kind of fall-off from a bad quarter alone.

chapters.label: 💻 Tech
chapters.text: Virginia and Oregon just became the first states to sue SpaceX over Grok. SpaceX bought Musk's AI company xAI in February, so it inherited the mess. The mess is Grok's rollout of a racy image feature that was quickly found to generate nonconsensual intimate images and sexual images of children. Musk's companies apologized and said they'd added safeguards. The states say that was misleading, and that Grok is still producing this material today. They allege the company chose to embrace sexualized content to grab AI market share. Virginia's attorney general put it plainly: once these images exist, they can never be fully erased. For its part, X says every Grok output is screened. The suits seek to cover every Grok or X user in each state. When a company's safety record gets compared to a sieve, the sieve usually looks better.

chapters.label: 🌍 World
chapters.text: NATO's chief, Mark Rutte, says the alliance will defend itself in space too, after German media reported that Russia is preparing to launch a satellite carrying a nuclear warhead. Public broadcasters NDR and WDR and the paper Süddeutsche Zeitung cite anonymous military and intelligence sources, who say it's called Sputnik-S and could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, like communications and observation ones. The reported timeline is the next sixty days. Putting nuclear weapons in orbit is something the Outer Space Treaty was written to prevent, by the way. Russia's embassy calls it propaganda, and the Kremlin says it hasn't even seen the reports. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz didn't confirm or deny, but said the reports show how much escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue. And honestly, naming it after the satellite that started the space race? That's a lot of nostalgia for a doomsday device.

chapters.label: 🇺🇸 U.S.
chapters.text: Video of a Saturday arrest at Seattle-Tacoma airport has gone viral, and now the family is talking. Masked ICE officers took Sofia Hernandez Mejia and her father, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, into custody at a jet bridge door. In the footage, she's wailing and saying she has a valid work permit, while bystanders demand answers. Her husband, Jose Castillo, is a US citizen, and he told CBS he felt useless, adding that it all happened so fast. Homeland Security says both are Mexican nationals who overstayed their visas, and that officers were targeting the father when other passengers began obstructing them. DHS also accuses Hernandez Mejia of assaulting agents by throwing hot coffee, and says she'll be charged. Castillo says she did nothing, she was being shoved, and when people come at you and shove you, coffee spills.

chapters.label: 🎬 Culture & Entertainment
chapters.text: Molly Meldrum has died at 83 after a long illness. If you're not Australian, he was the country's most beloved music guy: promoter, broadcaster, host of the ABC's Countdown, then a segment on Hey Hey, It's Saturday. He championed local acts like INXS and Kylie Minogue and international ones like Abba, and he was never without his Stetson hat. In 2014 he became the first non-recording artist inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame. King Charles called him a true giant of the music industry, and Elton John paid tribute too. Of course the royal link is the famous 1977 interview, when a nervous Meldrum told the then Prince Charles, oh, I'm sweating like a pig. Years later Charles joked that nobody had prepared him for Molly Meldrum. Which, honestly, is how you'd want to be remembered: by a king who's still laughing.

chapters.label: ⚡ Quick hits
chapters.text: Quick hits. Everton lost 4 to 0 at Brentford, with James Tarkowski sent off in the 40th minute after VAR upgraded a yellow to red. David Moyes said Tarkowski got the ball but admitted he could see why it was given, so that's a suspension problem on top of a thumping. The UN climate talks in Turkey, COP31, ended with no deal after the longest conference ever, because the final text didn't even mention fossil fuels. Thanksgiving travel is going to cost you: gas is 56 cents a gallon higher than last year, and airfare is up around 30 percent, though AAA still expects a near-record 81.5 million travelers. The first ever Children's Booker Prize has its eight-book shortlist and four kid judges, so the critics are officially twelve. And Bangladesh's ousted leader Sheikh Hasina says she'll come home December 16th. A government minister says she'll arrive in handcuffs, which is not the red carpet she was hoping for.

chapters.label: Wrapping up
chapters.text: That's your Tuesday. Go Spurs, fifteen and three, and may your Thanksgiving flight be cheaper than mine. Talk tomorrow.
